CODEBOOK A byte-pair tokenizer, set in Rust, agreeing with tiktoken to the last id
CodebookSend a message

Pay by the token.

Telegraph companies charged by the word, so businesses bought code books that swapped common phrases for single code words. A GPT tokenizer does the same with bytes: it learns which strings come up most and gives each one a number, and a language model reads, and bills, by the number. This one is written from scratch in Rust and runs in this page. It learned its book from IMDB reviews in half a second, and, loaded with GPT-4's book, it matches tiktoken token for token.

CodebookEntries 256 to 295

The first entries

The book starts with one entry per byte, 0 to 255. Training then keeps adding the most frequent adjacent pair, counted across all 25,000 reviews. These are the first forty additions and how often each pair occurred when it was chosen. A dot is a space.

The longest

After 32,512 additions, whole words have their own entry. The longest are the vocabulary of film criticism.

    CodebookNotes

    Notes on the book

    A book fits its text

    Nothing is unknown

    The book starts with all 256 bytes, so any text can be encoded, including emoji and scripts it never saw. They just cost more: a Chinese character it has no entry for takes three code words, one per byte. Try "three languages" on the first spread.

    The scanner

    Checked against minbpe

    Karpathy's lecture Let's build the GPT Tokenizer comes with a reference tokenizer in Python, minbpe. Trained on minbpe's own test text, with its rule for breaking ties, this book learns the same merges in the same order and writes the same model files.

    NotesRate table

    Codebook is project 08 of Evan Wilson's AI project run. Source, write-up and every number in this book: github.com/evannwilsonn/codebook.

    Set in Young Serif, Crimson Pro and IBM Plex Mono. The tokenizer is Rust compiled to WebAssembly. GPT-4's vocabulary is OpenAI's cl100k_base as published with tiktoken. Reviews from the IMDB Large Movie Review Dataset (Maas et al., 2011). Nothing you type leaves the page.
